key_insight: Optical-fiber daylighting can substantially cut vertical-farm lighting electricity use, but current fiber costs and crop-yield penalties keep it from being economically competitive with LEDs or rooftop PV.
engineering_relevance: The paper quantifies how solar concentration, fiber delivery, and daylight/LED hybridization trade off energy savings, crop productivity, and cost in controlled-environment agriculture.
method: Validated transient vertical-farm model coupled with Tonatiuh ray-tracing for a single-axis tracked Fresnel concentrator.
Compared five optical-fiber types and three daylighting strategies against light-pipe and rooftop PV baselines.
Evaluated useful-PAR delivery, specific electrical energy consumption (SEEC), crop output, and light cost.
evidence_signal: The optical-fiber system achieved 19–27% annual useful-PAR delivery efficiency, cut electricity use by 35–89% depending on configuration, and hybrid strategies reached about 50% savings with a minimum SEEC of 3.16 kWh kg^-1.
watch_item: Economic viability is currently limited by very high optical-fiber capital cost, with roughly a 90% cost reduction needed for competitiveness, and daylight-only operation can reduce crop productivity by 52%.
paper_title: Can sunlight replace LEDs in vertical farms? A critical assessment of optical-fiber daylighting strategies
